newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan opposition may heed Islamist boycott call.
newsitem.headline: Jordan opposition may heed Islamist boycott call.

text.p: Jordan's main secular opposition parties may pull out of November parliamentary elections in response to calls for a boycott by the influential Moslem Brotherhood, an opposition politician said on Thursday.

Ahmad Youssef, politburo member of the Jordan People's Democratic Party, said 10 pan-Arabist and leftist opposition groups would review their plans to stand in Jordan's first elections since a 1994 peace treaty with Israel.
"They will go back to their parties for renewed discussions on participation or boycott," said Youssef, who represented his party at a meeting on Thursday.

The Moslem Brotherhood, whose Islamic Action Front (IAF) political arm is Jordan's largest opposition party, said on Wednesday it would boycott the elections to protest against government steps which it said sidelined parliament and hurt democracy.

The IAF has not yet fallen into line with the Brotherhood edict. Some of its members say a boycott would be self-defeating, curbing Islamist political influence and handing the government yet more power.
The elections are due by November. No date has been officially set but the government has pledged they will be held fairly and on time.
Youssef said the opposition feared government interference.

"The decision to participate was dependent on guarantees ensuring that the elections would be free and democratic. The sword of boycott would be unsheathed if these guarantees were not made," he said.
"Until now there are no guarantees. Any decision to boycott, from the Brotherhood or the (other) opposition parties, will be the responsibility of the government."

The Brotherhood said its boycott was a response to "interim" laws issued by the government during parliament's recess, including tough press law amendments, election regulations which the opposition say favour pro-government tribal candidates, and economic reforms condemned by the opposition.

IAF spokesman Hamza Mansour said his party would decide on Saturday whether to ignore the Brotherhood ruling and go ahead with its election campaign, or refer the matter back to the IAF's consultative council for a review which could take weeks.

In the last elections in 1993 the Islamic Action Front won 16 of 80 seats in a parliament filled by small pro-government parties and tribal representatives. Together with other opposition members they sometimes mustered a voting bloc of 23.

But they failed to block ratification of Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel, which the opposition want cancelled, and supporters of the boycott said it was time to pull out of a parliament which they said they could not influence.
